The textbook interval $q \pm$1.645 se($q$) is symmetric by construction: it treats the estimator as normal with equal room on both sides. GARP says this breaks down for extreme quantiles. GARP: the symmetric intervals “are misleading for extreme quantiles whose ‘true’ confidence intervals are asymmetric reflecting the increasing sparsity of extreme observations as we move further out into the tail”.

loText: Apply the bootstrap historical simulation approach to estimate coherent risk measures.
question: A model validator at a Japanese trust bank is reviewing code that estimates a bootstrap historical simulation 99% VaR from 1,000 daily P/L observations in JPY. The code builds each of 5,000 resamples by randomly shuffling the order of all 1,000 original observations, computes the 99% VaR of each shuffled data set, and reports the mean of the 5,000 resample VaRs as the best estimate. Which of the following assessments is most accurate?

options.A: The procedure is valid, because random resampling followed by averaging the resample VaRs is the bootstrap, and the order of observations does not affect a VaR.
options.B: The procedure is flawed only because the median of the 5,000 resample VaRs, not their mean, is the natural bootstrap best estimate of VaR.
options.C: Every shuffled set contains each original observation exactly once, so all 5,000 VaRs equal the basic HS VaR; drawing with replacement is needed.
options.D: The procedure is flawed only because 5,000 shuffles are too few; with many more shuffles the resample VaRs would spread out as a bootstrap requires.

solution:
**Shuffling is not resampling**

Stem in one line: code shuffles all 1,000 JPY observations 5,000 times and averages the VaRs; assess it.

**Concept and theory**

The bootstrap works because each resample is a different draw from the empirical distribution. Drawing with replacement makes the composition of each resample vary: one resample may contain the worst loss twice, another may miss it. That variation produces a spread of resample VaRs, whose mean is the bootstrap point estimate and whose percentiles give a confidence interval.

HS VaR depends only on the set of values in the sample, not on their order: sort the losses and read the ($n$(1 $- \alpha$) + 1)th largest. Any rearrangement of the same 1,000 values therefore gives the same VaR.

question:
A senior risk analyst at a Canadian pension fund applies bootstrap historical simulation to 500 daily P/L observations. For illustration only, four resamples of 500 observations each are drawn. The table shows the six largest losses in each resample (CAD million, ranked from the largest). For the 99% level, VaR is the sixth-largest loss in a data set of 500 and ES is the average of the five largest losses.

| Resample | 1st | 2nd | 3rd | 4th | 5th | 6th |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 8.42 | 7.95 | 7.31 | 6.88 | 6.40 | 6.14 |
| 2 | 9.10 | 8.04 | 7.12 | 6.75 | 6.21 | 5.86 |
| 3 | 8.42 | 8.42 | 7.31 | 6.95 | 6.71 | 6.58 |
| 4 | 7.95 | 7.40 | 7.12 | 6.60 | 6.12 | 5.94 |

Basic historical simulation on the original 500 observations gives a 99% VaR of CAD 6.25 million and a 99% ES of CAD 8.02 million. Which of the following is closest to the bootstrap estimates of the 99% VaR and 99% ES?

options.A: VaR CAD 6.25 million; ES CAD 8.02 million
options.B: VaR CAD 6.04 million; ES CAD 7.42 million
options.C: VaR CAD 6.36 million; ES CAD 7.36 million
options.D: VaR CAD 6.13 million; ES CAD 7.36 million

solution:
**Bootstrap point estimates of VaR and ES**

Stem in one line: four resamples of 500 CAD losses; find the bootstrap 99% VaR and ES.

**Concept and theory**

Each resample gives its own VaR and ES. The bootstrap “best” estimate is the mean of the resample estimates (GARP §2.2; App. 2 eq. 2.14):

$$\hat{\theta}_{B} = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{i=1}^{B} \hat{\theta}_{B(i)}$$

where $\hat{\theta}_{B\text{(}i\text{)}}$ is the estimate (VaR or ES) from resample $i$ and $B$ is the number of resamples. The ES is bootstrapped in the same way: compute the ES inside each resample, then average those ESs. GARP’s illustration: basic HS gave 95% VaR 1.704 and ES 2.196 for data with true values 1.645 and 2.063; 1,000 resamples gave about 1.669 and 2.114, closer to the truth.

| Source | Cause | Reduced by |

HW therefore rescales each return by $\sigma_{T} /\sigma_{t}$, observation by observation, because each day has its own $\sigma_{t}$. solution:
**FHS extensions: many assets and longer horizons**

Stem in one line: which statement about extending FHS to a multi-asset portfolio and a ten-day horizon is accurate?

Multi-asset. Fit a multivariate GARCH (or AGARCH) to the vector of asset returns and standardise the vector.
